slides: Welcome back. Before the advanced questions, two short tools. The other tools you'll learn inside the questions that use them.

slides.say: First tool. If a number leaves a remainder, take the remainder away, and what's left divides exactly. Sixty-one divided by eight. Seven eights are fifty-six, so it leaves five. Sixty-one minus five is fifty-six, and that's seven times eight, no remainder.
Another one. Forty-seven divided by six. Seven sixes are forty-two, so it leaves five. Forty-seven minus five is forty-two, six times seven.
Why does it work? The remainder is the only part that doesn't divide. Take it away, and only full groups are left.
So when a question says a number leaves three when divided by four, you know that the number minus three divides by four. Fifteen leaves three, and fifteen minus three is twelve, three fours.
at: leaves three when divided by four

slides.say: Second tool. A number is divisible by four and by six. Does it have to be divisible by twenty-four? No. We need the smallest common multiple of four and six. Four is two squared, and six is two times three. Use each prime at its larger exponent, so two squared times three. That is twelve.

Twelve contains everything needed for division by four and by six, so multiplying twelve by any integer satisfies both conditions. So the number is a multiple of twelve, twelve k. Twelve, twenty-four, thirty-six, forty-eight, all divide by four and by six. Twenty-four k would miss twelve and thirty-six, and they do divide by both.
And when the two share nothing, just multiply. Divisible by three and by five is fifteen k, fifteen, thirty, forty-five. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
at: Divisible by three and by five
